learn.title: Questions inside questions and statements (embedded questions)
learn.html:
An indirect question is a question that goes inside another sentence. It is used to sound more polite or when you don't know something: Do you know…?, Can you tell me…?, I wonder…, I have no idea…, I don't know….

Key rule: inside the indirect question the order is that of a statement (subject + verb). There is no inversion and do / does / did disappear; the verb returns to its normal form and the tense is kept.

Direct questionIndirect question
What is the problem?Do you know what the problem is?
Where did you buy it?Can you tell me where you bought it?
What time does the store open?I wonder what time the store opens.
Is the battery charged?Do you know if the battery is charged?
  • With yes/no questions use if (also whether): I wonder if/whether it works.
  • If the main sentence is a question (Do you know…?) it ends with «?». If it is a statement (I don't know…) it ends with a period.
  • With subject questions the order does not change: Who called? → I don't know who called.

watch.wrong: Do you know where is the charger?
watch.right: Do you know where the charger is?
watch.why: In the indirect question the verb goes after the subject.

watch.wrong: I wonder what time does the store close.
watch.right: I wonder what time the store closes.
watch.why: No do/does: the verb returns to its normal form (closes).

watch.wrong: Do you know the battery is charged?
watch.right: Do you know if the battery is charged?
watch.why: A yes/no question needs if or whether.

watch.wrong: I don't know why did the screen go black.
watch.right: I don't know why the screen went black.
watch.why: No did: the past is in the verb (went).

learn.title: Separable phrasal verbs (turn it on, plug it in)
learn.html:
A phrasal verb is a verb + particle (on, off, up, down, in, away…) with its own meaning. Separable ones allow the object to go between the verb and the particle.

ObjectPossible positionsExample
Nounverb + particle + object or verb + object + particleTurn on the TV. / Turn the TV on.
Pronoun (it, them, me…)verb + pronoun + particle (required)Turn it on. / Plug them in.
  • Common ones: turn on/off/up/down, plug in, hook up, set up, print out, put on/off/away/down, pick up, look up, take apart, throw away.
  • With a pronoun never put the particle before it: turn off it is incorrect.
  • If the object is long it usually goes after the particle: Turn off the old laptop that I never use.

watch.why: An object pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.

watch.wrong: I looked up it in the manual.
watch.right: I looked it up in the manual.
watch.why: Look something up is separable: pronoun before the particle.
With them the particle goes at the end.

learn.title: how to, where to, what to + verb
learn.html:
After show me, tell me, know, no idea, wonder, explain, remember you can use question word + to + verb. It is a short form of the indirect question when the subject is general (you, I, one).

Long formShort form
Can you show me how I can turn it on?Can you show me how to turn it on?
Do you know where I should plug it in?Do you know where to plug it in?
Let me show you what you have to do.Let me show you what to do.
I don't know which button I should press.I don't know which button to press.
  • It works with how, where, what, which, when, who; not with why.
  • The particles of phrasal verbs keep their place: I don't know where to plug it in.
  • For yes/no meaning use whether to: I can't decide whether to buy it.

watch.wrong: Can you show me how to I turn it on?

watch.why: to + verb in the base form, without -ing.

learn.title: Giving a different opinion and finding agreement
learn.html:
To disagree politely:

  • I know what you mean, but… — I know what you mean, but you can make real friends online.
  • That's true. … , though. — That's true. It's still useful, though.
  • Maybe. On the other hand, … — Maybe. On the other hand, it saves time.
  • I don't know. / I'm not (so) sure. Don't you think …? — I'm not so sure. Don't you think it's better to talk face-to-face?

To ask the other person to agree with you: You know what I mean? / You know? / You know what I'm saying?

Useful vocabulary: spend time with someone, face-to-face, text (v.: send a text message), social networking site.

To plan an article: write all your ideas without worrying about grammar, choose the best ones, number them, then write and check spelling and grammar.

write.model:
Last month my phone suddenly stopped working, and I was in a panic. I didn't know why it had turned off, and I wondered if I had lost all my photos. Here is how I solved the problem, in case it ever happens to you.

First, I tried to turn it on again, but nothing happened. I plugged it in and left it for an hour. Then I looked up the problem on the internet and found out that the battery could be damaged. I asked a friend whether she knew where to get it repaired, and she told me about a small shop near my house. The technician asked me to back up my files, so I saved everything in the cloud and then turned it off before he started. He fixed it in two days.

I also realized I had not been careful with my online safety. I didn't know how to create a strong password, so I looked it up and changed all of mine. Now I use two-step verification and I never click on links from strangers, because scams are everywhere.

In conclusion, a technology problem can be stressful, but it is usually easy to solve. Ask yourself what you would do if you lost your data tomorrow. Remember to update your apps, and do not wait for an emergency to learn how to protect your accounts.

Don't you think…?) and mention one safety precaution.

At least 3 expressions for giving a different opinion
Two clear points of view with examples
One safety precaution (password, scam, shred…)
At least one well-formed indirect question
Paragraphs organized and revised
write.model:
Do social media and technology bring us closer or push us apart? I think the answer depends on how we use them.

On the one hand, many people believe that technology brings us together. I have friends who live in other countries, and I talk to them every week by video call. Thanks to social media, my grandmother, who is eighty, can see photos of her grandchildren every day. I know what you mean when people say it feels cold, but for families like mine it is a great help.

On the other hand, some people argue that social media pushes us apart. Maybe. We are often together at dinner, but everyone is looking at their phone. I'm not so sure that a hundred online friends are better than one real conversation. Don't you think we are losing the skill of listening? That's true for many young people, though not for everyone.

There is also a problem with safety. Many people share their personal information without thinking, and scams are becoming more common. One simple precaution is to use a strong password and never share it. I also wonder if companies are doing enough to protect our data.

In my view, technology is not good or bad in itself. What matters is how we use it, and whether we remember to put the phone down and look at the person in front of us.

reading.title: The day my phone died
paragraphs: Last Tuesday, my phone froze up in the middle of an important video call with a client in Guadalajara. I had no idea what the problem was. The screen went black, and when I turned it on again, nothing opened. I wondered if the battery was dead, so I plugged it in, but the charging light didn't come on. Then I realized I didn't know where the power cord I usually used was. After ten minutes of searching, I found it under a pile of old instruction manuals.

Eventually the phone started, but it was painfully slow. A coworker named Daniela, who is very tech-savvy, offered to help. "Do you know how much storage you have left?" she asked. I didn't know, so she looked it up in the settings and showed me what to do. My phone was almost full: hundreds of photos, three games I never play, and an app I couldn't even remember downloading. Daniela deleted the old files, took off the case, and ran antivirus software. She found a virus hidden in a free app, and she explained how it had probably gotten onto my phone.

"You should be careful with free apps," she said. "Some of them are scams. They steal your data, and in the worst cases someone can use your information to open an account in your name." She told me that I should never give away my password or my PIN, and that I should block suspicious emails instead of opening them. I had always thought these warnings were exaggerated. Now I know better, and I'm a little embarrassed that I needed a virus to learn the lesson.

Of course, not everyone agrees about technology. My brother says smartphones have ruined real conversation. I know what he means, but I think phones can also bring people closer. I talked to my grandmother in Oaxaca last week, and we saw each other face-to-face on a screen. On the other hand, I admit that I check my phone too often, and I'm not so sure that's healthy. He may be right about that, though.

Since that Tuesday, I've made a few changes. I back up my photos every Sunday, I turn my phone off at night, and I keep the power cord in a drawer where I can always find it. I also printed out a short list of safety tips and put it away next to my desk. It's a small list, but it can save me a lot of trouble: never click on strange links, update your apps, and ask for help when you don't know what to do. Technology is useful, but only if we learn how to use it carefully.
